title: Ethereum, Smart Contracts & Tokens
description: Ethereum is a public computer: accounts, EVM storage, ERC-20/BEP-20 as interfaces, gas, ABI, explorers, and the failures that empty wallets. BSC is EVM-family on chain 56 with BNB as fuel. Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 to verify, not tuition. Education only. Intermediate is $10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout.

modules.title: Ethereum as a computer
modules.description: A public machine with shared memory. Not Bitcoin with extra coins. Not a blessing.

lessons.title: A public computer, not a second Bitcoin
lessons.content:
# A public computer, not a second Bitcoin

Bitcoin is a public notebook of transfers under a tight rule: who may debit which unspent output. Ethereum, launched in 2015, is a **public computer that also keeps a notebook**. If you treat it as “Bitcoin with extra coins,” you will misread token rows, failed calls that still cost fuel, and every website that wants a signature.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name Ethereum as a machine — programs, shared memory, sealed pages — and say why a token transfer is a program rewrite rather than a native-coin handoff.

## A notebook versus a computer

A notebook records that value moved. A computer **follows instructions and remembers results**. Ethereum’s bet was: let anyone publish a small program, and let every honest node run that program the same way. The transfer notebook remains. The new object is the **program**.

That program is a **smart contract**. The name is a marketing accident. It is not a court document and it is not a handshake. It is **bytecode**. Honest nodes execute the same opcodes on the same inputs and arrive at the same next state. Courts still speak to companies and people. The chain does not parent you.

## State is the machine’s official memory

**State** is the official memory at a block: every account’s native balance, every contract’s stored slots. A wallet is a view of a few rows. An explorer is a larger view. Neither is the whole machine.

A native-coin transfer rewrites two balances in state. A **token** transfer usually does **not** move ETH from sender to receiver as the payment. It asks a token program to rewrite two numbers in **its** storage. You still pay the native coin as **gas** so the computer will do that rewrite.

## Native coin is fuel, not a souvenir

If fuel lived inside a token program, you would need that program to run in order to pay to run programs. A circle. **ETH** sits at protocol level on Ethereum mainnet (chain ID **1**). The protocol can charge gas even if every token contract is broken.

On **BNB Smart Chain** (chain ID **56**) the same family of computer uses **BNB** as fuel. Same-looking 0x addresses. Different books. Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 **on BSC**, not an ETH-native object. Identity is the 0x plus the chain ID, not the letters in a wallet dropdown.

TABLE
Object | Where it lives | Fuel to change it
ETH | Account balance on chain 1 | ETH
BNB | Account balance on chain 56 | BNB
USDT (token) | A mapping inside a USDT contract on that chain | Native coin of **that** chain
Crystal Stones | Mapping inside `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BSC | BNB — verify only, not tuition
ENDTABLE

## Public is not a blessing

Public means: anyone who can pay the fee can try to write; anyone can read. Scam programs run as calmly as useful ones. Legal tender is a government word. Unique is a marketing word. The machine does not sort them.

DIAGRAM
USER SIGNATURE
    --> transaction (to, data, gas, chainId)
        --> public computer (EVM)
            --> new state (balances, storage)
Explorer and wallet are views of that state, not the machine.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rails for this whole course: Intermediate is **$10 USDT BEP-20** on academy checkout — not Crystal Stones token, not a chat 0x. Crystal Stones at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BSC (chain ID 56) is **verify-only**. Gas on BSC is BNB. Staff never ask for a seed, key, 2FA, or remote control. This course will not tell you to buy anything.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Ethereum is a public computer plus a notebook.
- A smart contract is bytecode, not a lawsuit.
- Token rows live in a program’s storage.
- Fuel is the native coin of that chain.
- Same 0x letters on two chain IDs are two accounts.

Next: the EVM’s desk — stack, memory, storage.

lessons.title: The EVM desk — stack, memory, storage
lessons.content:
# The EVM desk — stack, memory, storage

Wallets draw flowcharts: connect, approve, swap. The processor that actually runs a contract is a **stack machine** with a scratch pad and a durable notebook. If you only learn the flowchart, gas and reverts will look like superstition.

By the end of this lesson you should place a number in stack, memory, storage, or calldata, and explain why a failed swap can still cost fuel.

## Four places a number can sit

**Stack.** Last-in, first-out words. Most opcodes pop arguments and push results. This is why “stack machine” is the honest picture of the EVM, not a flowchart of logos.

**Memory.** Temporary bytes for this call. It expands as the program writes. **It dies when the call ends.** Used to build return data, hash inputs, and copy calldata. Expanding memory costs gas on a curve. It is not a diary.

**Storage.** The contract’s durable slots in world state. `SSTORE` is expensive because every full node must remember the slot. Token balances live here. Owner addresses live here. Allowances live here. If you care whether a fact survives the next block, you are talking about storage.

**Calldata** is the input bytes of the transaction: function selector plus arguments. Cheap to read. It is not the contract’s notebook. It is the letter you posted.

TABLE
Place | Survives the call | Survives in state | Job
Stack | Only while running | No | Arithmetic and control
Memory | Until the call ends | No | Scratch
Storage | Yes | Yes | Balances, config, allowances
Calldata | As transaction history | Not “the contract’s notebook” | Selector + arguments
ENDTABLE

## Why this picture pays rent

“Failed but I paid gas.” Work ran. **Revert** undoes this call’s storage writes. Fuel for work already done still burns. The computer does not run for free because you did not like the result.

“The contract holds my USDT.” Your row is in the **token** contract’s storage. Another contract may have **allowance** to rewrite it. The pair you see in a wallet is not a vault with your name on the door. It is a mapping.

“Verified source.” Someone published text that compiles to this bytecode. That is a compiler match. It is not an audit, not a promise, not a mine.

## Calls inside calls

A contract can `CALL` another. Each inner call has its own memory. Storage is global to that contract. `DELEGATECALL` is the dangerous cousin: it runs *other* bytecode against **this** contract’s storage. Proxies are built on that trick. Module 6 returns to it. For now: if you cannot say whose storage is being written, you cannot say what you signed.

BNB Smart Chain runs an **EVM-compatible** processor. Compatible means the same family of bytecode and the same desk. It does not mean shared state with Ethereum.

DIAGRAM
CALLDATA --> EVM
              +-- STACK (plates)
              +-- MEMORY (dies at end of call)
              +-- STORAGE (world state)
              +-- nested CALL / DELEGATECALL
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: a revert is not a refund machine. If a site says “if it fails you pay nothing,” they are describing a different computer, or they are lying about this one.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Stack is scratch arithmetic.
- Memory dies. Storage is the notebook.
- Revert undoes writes, not gas.
- Calldata is the letter, not the diary.
- BSC is EVM-family, not Ethereum’s book.

Next: chain ID 1 versus chain ID 56 as geography.

lessons.title: Chain ID 1 versus chain ID 56
lessons.content:
# Chain ID 1 versus chain ID 56

Same address shape. Same wallet UI. Two computers. Intermediate fails the day you treat them as nicknames.

By the end of this lesson you should refuse to send until you can name asset, chain ID, bookmarked explorer, and fuel coin — four words, not a vibe.

## Two books, one alphabet

Ethereum mainnet is chain ID 1, fuel ETH, explorer of the Etherscan class, token interface nicknamed ERC-20. BNB Smart Chain is chain ID 56, fuel BNB, explorer of the BscScan class, token interface nicknamed BEP-20 (ERC-20-style). Crystal Stones as taught here lives on 56 at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`.

Copied: address shape, gas metering, ABI idea, wallet apps. **Not copied:** state, native coin, validator set, the actual deployed programs, explorer databases.

USDT on Ethereum is a row in Ethereum’s USDT contract. USDT on BSC is a row in a **different** contract. Ticker letters are not a network. Bridged assets are **new** contracts with their own allowance sets. Approving USDT on chain 1 does nothing to USDT on chain 56.

## Why chain ID is in the signature

EIP-155 put `chainId` into the signed payload so a transaction meant for one book cannot be replayed onto another. Wallets still let humans pick the wrong network in the dropdown. The signature will be valid **on the chain it names**. The funds you thought you moved may sit on a book you do not watch.

A **centralised exchange** withdrawal is a multiple-choice network question. Wrong choice, missing funds. Help desks cannot unwrite a public page. “USDT” in the withdrawal menu is not complete until chain ID is named.

## Cheap gas is a lure as well as a feature

BSC’s cheaper gas makes tiny practice possible. It also makes fake tokens cheap to spawn. Dear gas on Ethereum does not make a contract honest. Cheap gas does not make a contract honest. Honesty is not a fee schedule.

Paste the Crystal Stones 0x onto an Ethereum explorer and you are looking at a **different world** — empty, unrelated, or a copycat. Verification for this academy is **chain 56**, bookmarked origin, then paste.

TABLE
Before you send | Acceptable | Costume
Asset | Named contract 0x | “USDT” with no chain
Chain | 1 or 56 (or another you named) | “BSC (ETH)” in a chat
Explorer | Bookmarked origin | First search-ad result
Fuel | ETH on 1, BNB on 56 | “pay gas in CST”
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
WALLET DROPDOWN: "USDT"
        |
        +--> which chain ID?
        +--> which contract 0x?
        +--> which explorer origin?
        +--> which coin pays gas?
If any arrow is a shrug, do not send.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: four names before you send. Guessing one of them is how people fund a recovery-theatre second lesson. Staff will not unsend.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- 1 / ETH / Ethereum explorer. 56 / BNB / BSC explorer.
- Same letters, different books.
- Ticker is not a chain.
- Cheap gas is not honesty.
- Four names, then send.

lessons.title: What this course teaches and refuses
lessons.content:
# What this course teaches and refuses

By the last quiz you should be able to: split EOA from contract; say what a contract stores; name ERC-20 / BEP-20 as interfaces; read gas, ABI, and explorer tabs; list how this design empties wallets.

You will not be a Solidity developer, an auditor, a trader, or a recovery agent. Those are other jobs. This is a seeing course.

By the end of this lesson you should recite the refusals without looking, including the tuition rails.

## What “seeing” means

Seeing is: pointing at a function name, a storage idea, a chain ID, and a failure mode. It is not: deploying a protocol, issuing a security opinion, or opening a position because a lesson used a ticker as an example.

Practice, when asked, is amounts you can lose. Prefer a **testnet** when a later lesson says so — a practice computer with worthless play coins and **different state**. Testnet success is not mainnet safety.

## Hard refusals

No buy targets. No yield homework. No “Ethereum replaced banks.” No “green tick is an audit.” No paying Intermediate in Crystal Stones. No recovery DMs. Staff never want a seed, key, 2FA codes, or remote desktop.

Certificates in this academy are **academic**. Checkout is not a token purchase. Completing a quiz does not mint you a claim on a warehouse, a DAO, or a pool.

TABLE
Want | Get | Do not get
Web3 vocabulary | Objects and failure cases | A job offer
Pay Intermediate | $10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout | A CST invoice
Safety | How approvals, fakes, and proxies work | A magic undo
Practice | Optional tiny tests, preferably testnet | Assigned mainnet size
ENDTABLE

## Never-list, already

The never-list does not wait for Module 6. If a window asks for a seed phrase, a private key, an authenticator code, or remote screen control, it is not this academy. If a window asks you to pay gas in CST, it is not this academy. If a window offers to recover a drain, it is the second drain.

DIAGRAM
THIS COURSE
  teaches: accounts, storage, ERC-20/BEP-20, gas, ABI, explorer, drains
  refuses: entries, yield, recovery, CST as tuition or gas
CHECKOUT --> USDT BEP-20 on academy origin
VERIFY  --> CST 0x on chain 56, read-only
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: Mentor and staff do not recover funds. A “support” chat that starts after a failed transaction is not a help desk. It is a product.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Seeing course, not a shop and not a recovery firm.
- $10 USDT BEP-20 on checkout.
- Verify-only CST contract on chain 56.
- Green tick is not an audit.
- No seed, no 2FA, no remote, no CST-as-gas.

Next module: two kinds of accounts.

modules.title: Two kinds of accounts
modules.description: A key is the user, or code is the user. Explorers blur the difference on purpose.

lessons.title: EOA — a key is the user
lessons.content:
# EOA — a key is the user

An **externally owned account** is an address derived from a public key. Control is possession of the matching private key — or of a seed that can derive that key. There is no contract code that must approve your spend. The signature *is* the user.

By the end of this lesson you should explain nonce, seed-as-factory, and why a hardware device still depends on the computer not lying about the payload.

## What an EOA actually is

`msg.sender` of a simple wallet transaction is the EOA. The account has a **nonce** that orders its transactions. Replay on the same chain is “use this nonce again”; the network will not accept a second transaction with the same nonce from the same EOA. Replay across chains is what chain ID in the signature is for — you already met that.

The address is a hash of the public key, shortened into 0x plus twenty bytes. **EIP-55 checksum** mixed-case letters catch some typos. They do not catch malice, lookalike addresses, or a clipboard that swapped the middle.

## Seed is a factory

A BIP-39 phrase plus a derivation path (often BIP-44) can produce **many** EOAs. One leak is not “one address.” It is every derived account on every chain that phrase can reach. “I only used it for a test wallet” is not a compartment if the path is standard.

You cannot log out of an EOA. You stop possessing the key, or you do not. Changing an academy password does not rotate a chain key.

## Hardware does not make the computer honest

A hardware wallet keeps the key in the device. The computer still builds the transaction. The device signs **what it is shown**. If the computer lies about the spender, the destination, or the calldata, a hurried glance at an 0x prefix is how people bless a drain. Read destination and amount on the device screen. If the device cannot show the selector, slow down.

TABLE
Object | What it is | Failure
Private key | The signer | Leak, malware, photo of a paper backup
Seed phrase | Factory for many keys | One leak, many accounts
Nonce | Order of this EOA’s txs | Stuck nonce, replacement fee games
Checksum | Typo hint | Not a fraud detector
Hardware device | Key offline | Computer lies about the payload
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
SEED --> many EOAs (paths)
KEY  --> signature --> tx on one chainId
Device signs bytes. Bytes come from a host you must still distrust.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: staff will never ask you to type a seed “to sync the course.” Progress is a database row, not a chain account. Checkout does not collect keys.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- An EOA is a key, not a login.
- A seed is a factory, not a username.
- Checksum catches typos, not thieves.
- Hardware signs what the host proposes.
- You cannot log out of a key.

Next: contract accounts — code is the user.

lessons.title: Contract accounts — code is the user
lessons.content:
# Contract accounts — code is the user

A contract account has an address and **code**. It has no private key of its own. It does what its bytecode does when called. “The protocol” is this object plus whoever the code names as admin.

By the end of this lesson you should refuse the sentence “the contract decided” until you can name `msg.sender`, the function, and any owner/role that can change the function later.

## Where the address comes from

Ordinary `CREATE` derives the address from deployer plus nonce. `CREATE2` derives it from deployer, a salt, and init code — so the address can be known **before** deploy. Same 0x shape as an EOA. The difference is the code field.

Empty code means EOA (or a contract that self-destructed in old rules). Non-empty code means a program. A **proxy** is a program whose 0x is a forwarding shell; the logic lives at an implementation address. The 0x you see in a wallet may be the shell.

## Who is the user of a contract

When you call a contract, `msg.sender` is you (or the contract that called it). When the contract calls a token’s `transferFrom`, the token sees the **contract** as sender. That is how vaults move your allowance.

Admin is **not** “the community” unless the code says so with a governor you can point at. Admin is `owner()`, a role in AccessControl, a proxy admin, a timelock, or nothing if those slots are burned **and** no other role remains.

A contract can hold ETH/BNB and tokens. “The protocol owns it” means `balanceOf(contract)` is large. That inventory can vanish to a bug, an admin, or a migration. Self-custody of your EOA does not self-custody the pool.

TABLE
Question | EOA | Contract
Signer | Private key | No key; code + callers
Admin | You | Whoever code names
Can hold tokens | Yes | Yes
Can be a proxy shell | No | Yes
Upgrade | Change your key practices | `upgradeTo` if coded
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
YOU --call--> PROXY 0x
                 |
                 +-- DELEGATECALL --> implementation bytecode
                 +-- storage still on PROXY
Admin of proxy != owner() on implementation unless you read both.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: a contract cannot “sign as you.” It can pull from you if you approved it. Those are different sentences. The second one is DeFi’s login, next course.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Contract accounts have code, not a shared private key.
- Admin is a named role, not a feeling.
- The 0x you see may be a proxy shell.
- Inventory in a contract is the program’s, not yours.
- CREATE2 lets an address exist on a slide before deploy.

Next: explorers hide the difference on purpose.

lessons.title: Explorers hide the difference on purpose
lessons.content:
# Explorers hide the difference on purpose

Explorers are companies. They draw badges, names, token lists, and “similar contracts” so a human can survive a page of hex. None of that drawing is consensus.

By the end of this lesson you should treat tags as a hint to verify, not as a signature from the chain.

## What the page is allowed to invent

**Name tags** (“Binance 8”, “Uniswap Router”) are a database. They can be wrong, late, or spoofed in a phishing clone of the explorer. **Token lists** on an EOA are indexer opinions of ERC-20/BEP-20 `balanceOf`. A spam token with a famous name will show up because the contract says you hold it, not because you bought it.

**Contract** badges mean “this address has code” (or the indexer thinks it does). They do not mean safe. **Verified** means compiler match. **Creator** is the deployer EOA or factory, useful and still not a moral grade.

**Internal transactions** are value moved by `CALL`, not a simple transfer from your EOA. People miss them and think “I never sent that.” The notebook includes inner calls.

## Similar is not same

“Similar contract” tools compare bytecode. A honeypot can be similar to a famous token. A proxy can look empty (tiny dispatcher) while the implementation is huge. Always open the implementation 0x too.

Search ads impersonate explorers. Bookmark the origin on a calm day. Check the TLS name. Do not use the first result after a drain — that is when impersonators buy the ads.

TABLE
UI element | Source of truth? | Use
Name tag | No — company DB | A hint to confirm 0x
Token tab | Indexer | Hide spam; do not import bait
Verified badge | Compiler match | Read source; still not an audit
Internal txs | Indexer of CALLs | Explain “I didn’t transfer”
Similar contract | Heuristic | Never a reason to approve
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
CHAIN STATE  -->  NODE  -->  INDEXER  -->  EXPLORER UI
You can skip the last two and still read with a node. The UI is a courtesy.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: this school will not send you to a search bar after a scare. Bookmark explorers now. A panic Google is part of the drain kit.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Tags are a company database.
- Verified is a compiler match.
- Internal txs are still movement.
- Similar bytecode is not safety.
- Bookmark the explorer origin.

Next: custody — your key, their key, nobody’s key.

lessons.title: Custody: your key, their key, nobody’s key
lessons.content:
# Custody: your key, their key, nobody’s key

Three pictures get mashed into the word “wallet.” This lesson splits them so a login, a signature, and a burn address stop sharing a nickname.

By the end of this lesson you should classify a setup as self-custody, custodial, or code-custody, and say what “nobody’s key” would actually require.

## Self-custody

You hold the key. You can sign. You can lose the key. The chain will not reset it. Lost key = lost account. Support theatre cannot unwrite a public page. A hardware device is still this picture: you possess the signer.

Self-custody plus a drainer site is still empty. The failure is the signature, not the slogan. “Not your keys, not your coins” does not mean “your keys, therefore safe.” It means the failure moved.

## Custodial

An exchange or app holds keys. You have a **login**. Their insolvency, freeze, or phish is your risk. Withdrawals are requests, not protocol rights. The balance you see is a **company database row** — an IOU — until a withdrawal hits a public book.

Academy checkout does **not** take custody of your seed. The school stores email, progress, and an order. Staff never ask for a key. Progress is not a chain backup.

## Code-custody, and the phrase “nobody’s key”

A **multisig** is M-of-N keys. Still people. A smart wallet / account-abstraction account is a **contract as the account**; recovery modules are extra admin. Better than a single EOA if the code and the signers are real. Worse if the “vault” is a proxy the owner can drain.

“Nobody’s key” is a claim about a **burned owner** or a **locked LP**. It is true only if the burn address cannot spend **and no other role remains** — no proxy admin, no `mint`, no `pause` on a different slot, no hidden `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`. A sticker that says “renounced” while ERC-1967 admin is live is a costume. Module 6 returns to that sticker.

TABLE
Picture | What can spend | How it fails
Self-custody | Your signature | Lost key, or you signed a drain
Custodial (CEX) | The company’s keys | Freeze, insolvency, phished login
Multisig | M of N people | Collusion, lost shares, bad UI
Smart wallet | Modules the code names | Recovery module is extra admin
“Nobody’s key” | Nobody, if truly no role remains | You read the wrong contract
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
SPEND PATH
  your key ------> EOA
  their key -----> company ledger (login)
  M-of-N keys ---> multisig contract
  module keys ---> smart-wallet account
  no key --------> only if burn cannot spend AND no other role
Academy checkout sits off this diagram. It is an invoice, not a custodian.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy checkout does not take custody of a seed. If a window offers to back up the key as part of tuition, close it. Tuition is USDT BEP-20 on the academy origin.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Self-custody: you can sign, and you can lose the account.
- Custodial: a company IOU; withdrawal is a request.
- Multisig and smart wallets are still people plus code.
- “Nobody’s key” requires no remaining role, not a sticker.
- The academy is not a custodian of keys.

Next module: what a contract actually holds.

modules.title: What a contract holds
modules.description: Bytecode, storage, events, and the native coin people send by accident.

lessons.title: Bytecode versus source
lessons.content:
# Bytecode versus source

Nodes execute **runtime bytecode**. Source is optional publication. Wallets that show pretty function names are reading an ABI, which is also optional. The machine does not need your comments.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate compiler-match verification from an audit, and say why you must verify both a proxy and its implementation.

## What nodes actually run

When a call arrives, the EVM runs the bytes stored at that address. Those bytes may be a dispatcher that `DELEGATECALL`s elsewhere. Pretty GitHub is not in the state trie. If source is missing, you can still read selectors and storage; you are just working without the author’s names.

## What “verified” is

Verified, on an explorer, means: someone uploaded source and compiler settings that **reproduce** this bytecode (optimizer, via-IR, library links, compiler version). Get any of those wrong and the match fails. A match is not a review of economic design. It is not a review of admin keys. It is not a mineral assay.

## Proxy plus implementation

A proxy’s verified source is often a handful of fallback lines. The product lives at the implementation 0x. Verify **both**. Read ERC-1967 slots if the UI is cute. An implementation that is verified while the proxy admin can `upgradeTo` an unverified one tomorrow is a costume with a date.

## Closed source plus a poster

“Audit coming” is a poster. “Audited” is a PDF with a **scope**. Scope that skipped mint, proxy admin, or fee setters is a punchline. Unverified is not automatically malicious — some serious systems delay publication — but you then treat the ABI the UI shows as **untrusted captions**.

TABLE
Item | Means | Does not mean
Runtime bytecode | What the EVM runs | Safety
Verified source | Compiler match | Audit
ABI in a wallet | A caption of selectors | Completeness
Implementation 0x | Where logic lives for a proxy | Immutability
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
ADDRESS 0x
  runtime bytecode
     |
     +-- verified? compiler match or not
     +-- proxy? then also read implementation 0x + admin slot
Audit PDF sits off this diagram entirely.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: a green tick is not an audit. Do not pay tuition because a tick exists. Checkout is still USDT BEP-20.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Bytecode is the product.
- Verified is a compiler match.
- Verify proxy and implementation.
- Audit is a scoped PDF, or it is a poster.
- Unverified means you distrust UI captions.

Next: storage slots, mappings, and owner.

lessons.title: Storage slots, mappings, and ‘owner’
lessons.content:
# Storage slots, mappings, and ‘owner’

A contract has 2^256 storage slots. Compilers pack variables into them. `owner` in a simple Ownable often sits in slot 0. Mappings do not: they live at `keccak256(key . slot)`. If you cannot say where a privilege lives, you cannot say it was burned.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to find an owner or admin either via a public getter or by reading the slot the pattern uses, and refuse a renounce sticker that leaves another role alive.

## Read functions first

If the ABI has `owner()`, `getOwner()`, `hasRole`, or `admin()`, use them on the Read tab of a bookmarked explorer. Crystal Stones, as taught here, is a BEP-20 you **read** at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on chain 56. You do not send, approve, or pay tuition there.

## Slots when getters lie or missing

Proxy admin is often **not** `owner()` on the implementation. Transparent proxies use an admin slot (ERC-1967). UUPS uses `upgradeTo` on the implementation, gated by some owner. AccessControl uses `bytes32` roles; `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` is `0x00…0`. Count roles, not slogans.

## Renounce is a slot write

Setting owner to the zero address clears **that** Ownable slot. It does not clear a minter role, a pauser, a proxy admin, or a timelock proposer. A thread that says “renounced, so safe” without naming every remaining role is incomplete. Incomplete is allowed. “Safe” is not a word this course assigns.

## Who can change the slot

If `transferOwnership` still works, the privilege moves. If a timelock must queue that call, you have a delay, not a deletion. If an EOA can call it, you have a person. Write the 0x of that person in a memo dated today.

TABLE
Privilege | Where it often lives | How it dies
Ownable owner | Slot 0 or owner() | renounce / transfer to zero, if no other role
AccessControl admin | role mapping | revokeRole, if no other admin
Proxy admin | ERC-1967 admin slot | changeAdmin, if you found it
Minter | a role or mint() onlyOwner | unless a hidden mint remains
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
READ owner()
READ hasRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, x)
READ ERC1967 admin slot on proxy
If any of those is a live EOA or a skippable timelock, a person remains.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: you are not assigned to storage-dump a random token for size. You are assigned to know that stickers are not slots.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Privileges live in slots and roles.
- Renounce clears one slot.
- Proxy admin is a different 0x.
- Read CST; do not pay it.
- Date the memo; slots change.

Next: events are receipts, not promises.

lessons.title: Events are receipts, not promises
lessons.content:
# Events are receipts, not promises

The EVM can `LOG` bytes. Indexers turn those logs into pretty Transfer histories. A contract can omit a log, emit a log that does not match storage, or emit a “Transfer” that is not ERC-20. The chain’s truth for a balance is still `balanceOf`.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to prefer storage over an event feed when they disagree, and name what an event is for (indexers, not courts).

## What a log is

Events are cheap-ish receipts for off-chain watchers. `Transfer(from, to, amount)` is a convention, not a law of physics. A fee-on-transfer token may emit the pre-fee amount. A rebase token may change balances with no Transfer at all. If your wallet “history” is an event feed, it can be a costume of the mapping.

## Indexers are companies

Explorer token tabs and portfolio apps subscribe to logs. They can lag, drop, or mis-decode. They can also be the only reason a spam airdrop appears in your UI. Hiding unknown tokens is not rudeness. It is refusing to let an indexer set your next signature.

## Promises that never log

“We will list,” “we will burn quarterly,” “we will drop NFTs” are not events. They are marketing. If a team later emits a Burn event from an EOA, that is still just a send. True `burn` decrements `totalSupply`. You will do that subtraction in Tokenomics. Here: do not confuse a log with a duty.

TABLE
Signal | Grade | If it disagrees with storage
balanceOf | On-chain fact | Storage wins — it is storage
Transfer event | Receipt for indexers | Ignore the feed
Tweeted burn | Marketing | Not a log
“Will list” | Marketing | Not a log and not a listing
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
tx --> SSTORE (balances)
    --> LOG Transfer (optional, maybe lying)
Indexer --> wallet history
If the two forks disagree, believe SSTORE.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: a pretty history tab is not a court transcript and not a vault. It is a company’s view of logs.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Events are logs for indexers.
- Storage is the balance.
- Fee and rebase tokens break naive feeds.
- Marketing is not an event.
- Hide spam; do not import it.

Next: payable, fallback, and accidental native coin.
## Worked mismatch

A dashboard shows you received 1,000 of a token. `balanceOf(you)` returns 950. The missing 50 was a transfer tax the event ignored, or a rebase, or an indexer lag. You do not argue with the dashboard. You argue with the mapping. If you then approve a spender based on the dashboard integer, you approved a story.

Off-chain “we emitted a Burn” threads are the same family: a log without a matching `totalSupply` decrease is a send to somewhere, maybe a dead address someone still controls. Tokenomics will subtract two snapshots. This lesson only needs the reflex: log versus slot.

lessons.title: Payable, fallback, and accidental native coin
lessons.content:
# Payable, fallback, and accidental native coin

People send BNB or ETH to a token contract because the UI said “deposit.” Token mappings do not credit native coin. Unless the contract has `receive`/`fallback` **and** a withdraw path, the native units sit in the contract’s balance and nobody’s token row moved.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to refuse to treat a native send as a token purchase, and name wrap (WBNB) as a different, deliberate contract.

## Two different assets

Native coin is an account balance at protocol level. A BEP-20 is a mapping inside a program. `approve` does not take payable ETH as the token. Confusing them is how people “buy” nothing and then sign a second transaction to “fix it.”

## receive and fallback

`receive() external payable` runs on empty calldata. `fallback` runs otherwise. If they are missing, a direct native send reverts — good. If they exist but only increment an internal accounting the UI does not show, you donated. Recovery requires a `withdraw` the admin can call, or it requires a miracle. Many tokens have neither.

## Wrapping is explicit

WBNB/WETH is a wrapper: deposit native, mint 1:1 wrapped ERC-20; withdraw burns wrapped and returns native. Canonical wrapper 0x from a bookmark. Fake wrappers with the same name() are donations. Wrapping is not tuition and not a CST function.

TABLE
Action | What should move | Common failure
transfer(token) | Token mapping | Wrong 0x
approve | Allowance mapping | Infinite spender
send native to token 0x | Often nothing useful | Stuck native
wrap | Native -> WBNB 1:1 | Fake wrapper 0x
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
NATIVE BNB --> (wrong) token contract --> stuck
NATIVE BNB --> (right) WBNB.deposit --> WBNB mapping
Never: native send as 'paying Intermediate'. Checkout is USDT BEP-20.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: accidental native coin in a token contract is not a support ticket this school can reverse. It is a reason to slow down before the next send.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Native coin is not a token row.
- Payable fallback can trap BNB.
- Wrap only the canonical wrapper.
- Approve is not a payable buy.
- Checkout still is not CST.

Next: the ERC-20 / BEP-20 costume.
## Worked send

You meant to wrap BNB. You pasted the token 0x into the send field because the wallet’s ‘token’ and ‘native’ sit in one dropdown. 0.2 BNB arrives at the token contract. `balanceOf(you)` on the token did not increase. The contract has no `withdraw`. The 0.2 is the contract’s native balance. Support cannot unsend it. The only lesson left is the dropdown.

Wrapping, when you do it on purpose, is `deposit` on the canonical WBNB/WETH — bookmark that 0x the same way you bookmark USDT. Fake wrappers advertise the same name().

quiz.option_b: Compiler settings reproduce the bytecode

quiz.question: Token balances usually sit in?
quiz.option_b: The token contract’s storage mapping

quiz.question: Events are?
quiz.option_b: Logs indexers read; storage can disagree

quiz.question: Sending BNB to a token contract that has no withdraw usually?
quiz.option_b: Pays Intermediate tuition
quiz.option_c: Sticks native coin in the contract

quiz.question: Renounce of Ownable owner?
quiz.option_a: Deletes every admin role on every contract
quiz.option_b: Clears that owner slot; other roles/proxy admin may remain

quiz.question: DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in AccessControl is commonly?
quiz.option_b: bytes32(0)

quiz.question: WBNB wrap is?
quiz.option_b: Deposit of native BNB into a wrapper contract, 1:1 minus nothing but gas

quiz.question: If storage and a Transfer event disagree, prefer?
quiz.option_b: A Telegram screenshot

modules.title: ERC-20 and BEP-20
modules.description: A costume of functions. Tokens that break it. Importing is not minting. Allowances you forgot.

lessons.title: The ERC-20 costume
lessons.content:
# The ERC-20 costume

ERC-20 is an **interface**: `totalSupply`, `balanceOf`, `transfer`, `approve`, `allowance`, `transferFrom`, plus `Transfer` and `Approval` events. BEP-20 is that costume on BSC, sometimes with `getOwner`. The costume is not a mine, not a court, not tuition.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name the six functions, treat decimals as a display hint, and verify Crystal Stones as a BEP-20 costume on chain 56 without sending.

## Functions, not personality

`transfer` rewrites two mapping rows. `approve` writes `allowance[you][spender]`. `transferFrom` spends that allowance. `totalSupply` is the current integer, not a whitepaper max. If a UI button does not map to one of these (or to an obvious extra like `mint`), decode the selector before you bless it.

## Decimals are display

The contract stores integers. `decimals()` says how to draw them. USDT-class often uses 6; many tokens use 18. Mixing them in a spreadsheet concatenates a fantasy. Tokenomics returns to this. Here: never confuse raw units with the number on a poster.

## Return bool versus revert

The spec wants a boolean `true`. Some older USDT-class tokens on Ethereum return nothing and revert on failure. Routers that `require(token.transfer(...))` can break. This is a costume tear, not a mystery. BEP-20 on BSC usually reverts. Still read.

## Crystal Stones as a costume

This academy’s verification 0x is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on chain 56. Open Read. Confirm the interface exists. Extra functions (`mint`, `pause`, `blacklist`) are the real story. Verification is not a purchase and not Intermediate payment.

TABLE
Name | Job
balanceOf(addr) | Integer in the mapping
transfer(to, amt) | Rewrite two rows
approve(spender, amt) | Write standing pull-right
allowance(owner, spender) | Read that right
transferFrom | Spender pulls
totalSupply | Current units, not a slide
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
UI BUTTON 'swap'
   --> ? selector
        +-- transfer / transferFrom / approve / something else
If you cannot name it, do not sign.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: a costume match is the start of reading, not the end of risk.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- ERC-20/BEP-20 is an interface.
- Decimals are display.
- Identity is chain plus 0x.
- CST is a costume to read.
- Approve is a gun, next lessons.

Next: tokens that break the costume.
## What the costume is for

The costume exists so routers, wallets, and explorers can treat thousands of programs as one shape. That convenience is why a fake USDT works as UI: it also has `transfer`. Literacy is seeing the extra functions hanging off the costume — `mint`, `pause`, `setFee`, `blacklist` — and not stopping at `symbol()`.

Return-value tears (USDT-class on Ethereum) are why some routers special-case tokens. You do not need to memorise which live USDT behaves how. You need to know the tear exists so a revert is not ‘the chain is down.’

lessons.title: Tokens that break the costume
lessons.content:
# Tokens that break the costume

The interface is a costume. Authors add taxes, pauses, blacklists, rebases, and sell-reverts. The wallet still draws a logo. Intermediate reads the extra functions.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to list fee-on-transfer, rebase, pause, blacklist, and honeypot as costume tears, and say why a name() string is not identity.

## Fee-on-transfer

A tax on `transfer` means the recipient’s increase is smaller than `amount`. Routers that assume 1:1 then revert or leave dust. Sell-only taxes (`if(to==pair) fee=high`) are a cousin of honeypots. Read `setFee` — if owner can move 2% to 99%, the current 2% is a date, not a law.

## Rebasing and elastic

Balances change without Transfer. Lending markets that treat the token as static collateral can lie about health. You do not have to use these. You have to see them when `balanceOf` moves while you slept.

## Pause, blacklist, honeypot

`pause` can block `transfer` to a pair — you cannot sell — while excluded addresses still move. Blacklist is a freeze; USDT-class tokens disclose a company product; a meme with a hidden blacklist is the same function without the disclosure. Honeypot: buys work, sells revert unless `msg.sender` is excluded. You learn this from source or from a tiny failed sell, not from a candle.

## Names are stickers

`name()` and `symbol()` are strings. Anyone can deploy “USDT” or “Crystal Stones” on BSC. Identity is the 0x on chain 56 in academy materials, not the sticker. Fake CST is expected. Do not import it. Do not approve it.

TABLE
Tear | What you see | What to do
Fee-on-transfer | received < amount | Do not use naive routers
Rebase | balance moves with no Transfer | Do not treat as static collateral
Pause | transfers revert | You cannot exit through the pair
Honeypot | sell reverts | Tiny test or skip
Lookalike name | famous sticker, wrong 0x | Bookmark canonical 0x
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
transfer(amount)
   +-- tax? recipient gets less
   +-- pause? revert
   +-- blacklist? revert for you, not for them
   +-- honeypot? sell path reverts
Candle cannot show this. Source and a failed sell can.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: this course will not assign a honeypot hunt for size. Seeing the tear is the grade.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- The costume can lie.
- Taxes and pauses are functions.
- Honeypot is a sell-revert.
- name() is not identity.
- Canonical CST 0x is in academy materials.

Next: importing a contract into a wallet.

lessons.title: Importing a contract into a wallet
lessons.content:
# Importing a contract into a wallet

Wallet “import token” adds a **display watcher**. It does not mint a balance. It does not make a fake USDT real. It does not enroll you in Intermediate.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to treat import as a UI bookmark, and refuse to import bait airdrops or chat-pasted 0x addresses.

## What import does

The wallet will call `decimals`, `symbol`, `balanceOf(you)` on that 0x and draw a row. If `balanceOf` is zero, you see zero. If a scammer airdropped 5,000,000 of a lookalike, you see 5,000,000. The row is not a reason to tap it.

## Canonical 0x per chain

USDT on BSC is one 0x. USDT on Ethereum is another. Crystal Stones as taught here is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on 56. Import from academy materials or from a bookmark you made on a calm day. Import from a chat is how lookalikes get a seat on your home screen.

## Airdropped rows

Hide unknown tokens if the wallet allows. Do not follow a URL in the token name. Do not “claim” from that row. The claim site is the next lesson’s drain, wearing a token costume.

TABLE
Action | Changes chain state? | Safe use
Import token | No | Bookmark a canonical 0x
Hide token | No | Spam hygiene
Add from chat | No | Usually bait
Approve after import | Yes | Only if you meant the spender
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
AIRDROP --> wallet row (indexer + balanceOf)
         --> you tap 'claim'
              --> approve / drain
Import did not cause the drain. The signature did.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: importing CST from academy text is still verify-only. Importing does not pay Intermediate. Checkout is USDT BEP-20.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Import is a watcher.
- It does not mint.
- Canonical 0x per chain.
- Hide airdrops.
- Never claim from a spam row.

Next: allowances you forgot.
## Academy import versus chat import

If you import Crystal Stones, the only 0x this school will name is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on chain 56. After import you should see whatever `balanceOf(you)` actually is — often zero. Zero is not a failure of the course. The course is verification, not a drop.

A chat 0x with a similar name that shows a huge balance is the airdrop-to-approve path. Hide it. Do not add it to a watchlist you tap when hurried.

## Watchlist hygiene

A wallet watchlist is a local preference. Clearing it does not burn tokens. Adding a token because a group chat said ‘import this 0x to see the airdrop’ is how lookalikes get a tap target. If you need CST on screen, import the academy 0x once, on chain 56, and do not add cousins.

lessons.title: Allowances you forgot
lessons.content:
# Allowances you forgot

`approve(spender, amount)` writes a standing pull-right. The swap UI needed it for one `transferFrom`. The mapping does not expire when the swap UI closes. DeFi course loads this gun fully. Here you meet it as an ERC-20 fact.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to read allowance(you, spender), explain infinite approve, and revoke with approve(spender, 0) on the token Write tab.

## Standing, not a coupon

Until you set the allowance to 0 (or a new finite number), the spender may `transferFrom` up to that amount. `type(uint256).max` is about 1.16e77. No ERC-20 balance will spend it down. It is not “until this swap finishes.” Some USDT-class tokens require `approve(0)` before a new non-zero — a quirk, not a reason to leave max forever.

## Permit

EIP-2612 `permit` is a **signature** that writes allowance without an approve transaction. Phishing loves it: the site says “sign to log in” or “sign to vote.” Decode typed data. If it names a token and a spender, it is an approve in a hat.

## How to revoke without a helper

On the token’s Write tab, `approve(spender, 0)`. Then Read `allowance` to confirm. Batch-revoke helpers are extra contracts with extra admin. If you have two dirty spenders, skip the helper. Crystal Stones: do not approve CST to a “course router.” There is no course router.

TABLE
Pattern | What it writes | Hygiene
approve(router, max) | Infinite pull-right | Revoke after, or never max
approve(0) then new | USDT-class quirk | Still revoke later
permit(...) | Allowance via signature | Parse typed data
setApprovalForAll | NFT cousin, later course | Different gun, same never-list
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
YOU --approve--> SPENDER
SPENDER --transferFrom--> your mapping
Revoke: approve(spender, 0)
Helpers are optional and are extra trust.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: leftover router approvals are ordinary. Leaving them forever because a helper site looks busy is how last year’s listing drains this year’s mint.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Allowance is standing.
- Max is not ‘this swap’.
- Permit is approve by signature.
- Revoke on the token Write tab.
- No CST course-router.

Next: gas, ABI, and explorers.
## Two-chain leftover

You revoked a router on Ethereum. You still have max allowance on BSC USDT to a different router 0x. Approvals do not teleport. Bridged assets are different contracts. DeFi course will labour this. Here: after any lab, Read `allowance` on the **token you actually used** on the **chain ID you actually used**.

Permit leftovers are worse because you may not remember a transaction — there wasn’t one. Wallet activity labelled ‘signature’ is the place to look.

quiz.question: ERC-20/BEP-20 is best named as?
quiz.option_b: An interface of functions and events

quiz.question: decimals is?
quiz.option_b: A display hint; balances are integers

quiz.question: Fee-on-transfer breaks routers that assume?
quiz.option_b: amount received equals amount sent

quiz.question: Importing a token into a wallet?
quiz.option_b: Pays tuition
quiz.option_c: Adds a display watcher for that 0x

quiz.question: allowance is?
quiz.option_b: A standing pull-right for a spender until changed

quiz.question: type(uint256).max approve means?
quiz.option_b: Until you set 0 (or the token’s quirk requires 0 first)

quiz.question: Permit (EIP-2612) is dangerous because?
quiz.option_b: A signature can write allowance without an approve transaction

quiz.question: The identity of a token is?
quiz.option_b: Its Telegram

modules.title: Gas, ABI, explorers
modules.description: Metering, 4-byte selectors, the tabs that matter, and the tiny-test ritual.

lessons.title: Gas is metering, not a tip jar only
lessons.content:
# Gas is metering, not a tip jar only

Gas is how the public computer charges for work. You set a **limit**. You pay **base fee + tip** (names vary by chain). Unused gas can return. Work already done does not return because you reverted.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain why a failed swap can still cost BNB, and refuse any story that gas is paid in CST.

## The bill

Units of work × price per unit. Storage writes dominate. `approve` plus `swap` is two transactions, two bills, unless a permit packed them. Out-of-gas is a different failure from a `revert` with a reason string. Wallet “failed” is not a diagnosis until you read the status and the trace.

## Estimates are guesses

`eth_estimateGas` is a node simulating now. State can change before you land. A token with a tax flip can estimate clean and revert dirty. Treat estimates as weather, not law.

## Fuel is native

Ethereum mainnet: ETH. BSC: **BNB**. Not USDT. Not Crystal Stones. A DM that needs CST to “unlock gas” or “validator sync” is the never-list wearing a fuel hat. Academy checkout is USDT BEP-20 for tuition, which is also not gas.

TABLE
Term | Meaning
Gas limit | Max work you allow
Base fee + tip | Price of that work (names vary)
Revert | Undoes writes; work already done still bills
Out of gas | Hit the limit
Fuel coin | ETH on 1, BNB on 56
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
TX
  work (SSTORE, CALL, LOG)
  --> bill in native coin
  revert? writes undone, bill remains for work done
CST is not on this diagram.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: nobody from this school will ask you to send CST or BNB to a ‘gas station’ address in chat.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Gas meters work.
- Revert still bills work done.
- Fuel is native coin.
- Estimates are guesses.
- CST is not gas.

Next: ABI and the 4-byte selector.
## Failed and still billed — numeric

A swap estimates 200,000 gas. It runs 180,000 then reverts on slippage. You pay 180,000 × price. That is not theft by the chain. That is the meter. Setting 50% slippage ‘so it goes through’ is how you pay the meter **and** a sandwich. Markets course will name that. Here: the bill and the fill are different objects.

Gas station DMs that want CST or extra BNB to a chat 0x are never this academy. Fuel stays in your EOA until the protocol charges it on a tx you signed.

lessons.title: ABI and the 4-byte selector
lessons.content:
# ABI and the 4-byte selector

The first four bytes of calldata are usually `keccak256("function(type,type)")[:4]`. `transfer(address,uint256)` is `0xa9059cbb`. A wallet button labelled Swap is some selector on some router. The label is not the selector.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to decode a selector as the start of reading calldata, and distrust crowdsourced 4-byte directories as holy books.

## Why four bytes

Collision is possible but the convention holds. The rest of calldata is ABI-encoded arguments. A drain can use `transfer` on a token you did not intend, or `transferFrom` after a permit you thought was a login.

## UI names versus bytes

‘Swap’, ‘claim’, ‘list’, ‘vote’, ‘enable NFT’ are captions. Read the destination 0x and the selector. If the destination is a token and the selector is `approve` or `permit`, you are loading a gun, not swapping.

## Directories

4byte.directory-class sites are crowdsourced. They can be wrong or colliding. Verified source on the destination 0x is better. If the contract is unverified, you are signing unknown bytes. That can be a choice. It is not a confused one if you name it.

TABLE
Caption | Often really | Check
Swap | router selector | destination 0x vs bookmark
Claim | mint, or transferFrom of USDT | decode
Sign in | permit / typed data | token + spender
Vote | castVote, or permit | governor vs token
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
calldata = selector (4 bytes) + args
Wallet shows a caption.
You are signing the bytes.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: if calldata is huge and the caption is one word, slow down. This school will not ask you to sign unknown bytes to ‘unlock a lesson.’
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Selector is 4 bytes of a hash.
- Captions are not selectors.
- approve/permit are guns.
- Directories are crowdsourced.
- Unverified means unknown bytes.

Next: explorer tabs that matter.
## A worked caption

The button says Claim. Calldata starts `0x23b872dd` — `transferFrom(address,address,uint256)` — destination is USDT, not the NFT you thought. You were not claiming a mint. You were approving a pull with extra steps, or executing a pull you already approved. Decode before the hardware click.

`0xa9059cbb` is `transfer`. If the destination is your token and the `to` is not the person you named, you are donating. Captions will not save you.

## Selector plus destination

Always pair the 4 bytes with the `to` field. `0xa9059cbb` on USDT is a USDT transfer. The same 4 bytes on a random token is a random transfer. Hardware screens that show only ‘transfer’ without the token 0x are incomplete; abort if you cannot name the token.

lessons.title: Explorer tabs that matter
lessons.content:
# Explorer tabs that matter

A bookmarked explorer is a view. The tabs that pay rent are Code, Read, Write, Events, Holders — each with a grade. Analytics cartoons are the lowest grade.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to open Code (proxy + implementation), Read the privileges, and treat Holders as an indexer’s view.

## Code

Verified source, constructor args, implementation link, similar-contract noise. Similar is not same. Proxy: click through. Compiler version is part of the match.

## Read / Write

Read is `eth_call` and usually safe. Write is a transaction and costs fuel and can drain you. Connect-wallet on Write is how people bless a lookalike explorer. Bookmark first. Write `approve(0)` belongs here when you revoke.

## Holders and method column

Holders is indexer opinion plus labels. Concentration is still useful: one EOA with 90% is a fact worth dating. Method column on tx lists is decoded captions — same warning as ABI. Token tracker page versus address page: wrong tab, wrong book.

TABLE
Tab | Grade | Trap
Code | Compiler match | Skipping implementation
Read | eth_call | Trusting names without 0x
Write | Real tx | Lookalike explorer
Holders | Indexer | Labels as consensus
Analytics | Cartoon | Volume as truth
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
BOOKMARK origin
  Code --> proxy? implementation?
  Read --> owner, pause, mint, tax
  Holders --> concentration, dated
Write only when you mean a tx.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: do not use a search ad as an explorer after a scare. That slot is paid for by drainers.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Bookmark the origin.
- Code includes implementation.
- Read is a call; Write is a tx.
- Holders lag and label.
- Analytics is a cartoon.

Next: simulate, tiny test, then size.
## Proxy click-through as a habit

Token page → Contract → Read as Proxy (or implementation link). If that control is missing, you may be on the implementation already — or on an unverified shell. Holders on the token tracker is not the same list as internal ETH/BNB holders of the address. Wrong tab, wrong inventory.

Write tab plus a lookalike domain is a drain with extra UX. Confirm origin every session, not once in a lifetime.

## Labels versus holders

A holder labelled ‘Lock’ is an indexer guess. Click the address: is it a locker contract with time and no owner withdraw, or an EOA with a nickname? Tokenomics and DeFi will reuse this click. Here it is already an Ethereum habit: labels are not slots.

lessons.title: Simulate, tiny test, then size
lessons.content:
# Simulate, tiny test, then size

A wallet simulation (`eth_call` against pending state) can say success. So can a drainer. Simulation is not a conscience. A tiny test transfer proves that **that** path worked **once** at **that** size. It does not prove the next selector.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to order the ritual as read, simulate, optional tiny test — and say this course does not require a mainnet spend.

## Read first

Most of Intermediate is Read-tab literacy. You can finish this course without sending a mainnet transaction. That is allowed and often wiser.

## Then simulate

If you still intend a tx, simulate. If it fails, stop. If it succeeds, you have a guess. Check destination and selector anyway. A success-simulating drain is ordinary.

## Tiny test, then stop

A tiny native or token send to an address you control tests the **network and asset** choice, not the dapp. Testnets: different state, faucets, still public, still phishable. Prefer them when a later course says practise. Never size up because a testnet faucet was generous.

TABLE
Step | Proves | Does not prove
Read source/slots | What the code can do | That you should do it
Simulate | This call against now | Future state, morality
Tiny self-send | Chain ID + asset choice | The next dapp selector
Mainnet size | Nothing this school assigns | —
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
READ --> SIMULATE --> (optional) TINY SELF-SEND
This course's grade does not include mainnet size.
Tuition remains USDT BEP-20 on checkout, not a test swap.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: no assigned mainnet spend. If you insist on practising, use money you can lose and still read the selector.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Read first.
- Simulation is not a conscience.
- Tiny test is chain+asset, not the dapp.
- Testnet ≠ mainnet.
- No assigned size.

Next: how this design empties wallets.
## What a self-send is for

0.001 BNB to an address you control on chain 56 tests: network choice, clipboard, fuel. It does not test a router. After that, if you still want to touch a dapp, you are in DeFi’s lab rules — tiny, optional, money you can lose. This Ethereum course’s quiz does not require it.

Testnet faucets are public. Phishers wait there too. A green tick on a testnet explorer is still just a compiler match.

## Optional is optional

Skipping mainnet practice does not fail this course. The quizzes ask objects, not tx hashes. If a clone site requires a swap to ‘mark the lesson complete,’ it is not this academy. Progress is a login row after checkout in USDT BEP-20.

modules.title: How this design empties wallets
modules.description: Unlimited approvals, lookalike addresses, proxy stickers, and support theatre.

lessons.title: Unlimited approvals and drainers
lessons.content:
# Unlimited approvals and drainers

A site draws a swap. Calldata is `approve(max)` on a token, or a permit, and later `transferFrom` from a spender you did not bookmark. The UI logo is not a function.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to match the spender 0x against a bookmark, and treat infinite allowance as a loaded gun until revoked.

## The sequence

Connect → sign approve or permit → later, while you sleep, spender pulls. Sometimes both happen in one transaction via a helper. Sometimes the UI shows Swap and the first signature is approve. Read the destination. If it is the token, not the router you bookmarked, stop.

## IncreaseAllowance and cousins

Some tokens use `increaseAllowance` to avoid the 0-then-set quirk. The result is still a standing right. NFT `setApprovalForAll` is the cousin you will meet in the NFT course — one operator, every id, including future ids.

## Clone UIs

Drainers clone famous AMMs, NFT markets, and even ‘academy’ pages. TLS name, origin, spender 0x. Checkout for this school is the academy origin and USDT BEP-20. There is no CST router for a lesson.

TABLE
Signature | You think | Often is
Swap | Router swap | approve(max) on a token
Sign in | Login | permit
Claim airdrop | Mint | transferFrom USDT
Enable NFT | Listing | setApprovalForAll
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
BOOKMARK spender 0x on a calm day
PANIC UI  --> different spender --> drain
Revoke is approve(spender, 0) on the token.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: leftover max approvals are ordinary hygiene, not a moral failing. Leaving them because revoke ‘looks advanced’ is how last year’s lab becomes this year’s empty mapping.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Infinite approve is standing.
- Captions are not selectors.
- Match spender 0x to a bookmark.
- Permit is approve.
- No CST lesson-router.

Next: fake tokens and lookalike addresses.
## One-transaction drainers

Some helpers take approve-and-pull in a single user operation. Simulation can show success because the pull is the success. The bookmark of the spender still has to match. If the helper contract is unverified, you are signing unknown bytes that happen to be labelled Swap.

Revoke does not unsend what already left. It stops the next pull. Do it on the token, dated, and Read allowance after.

## After the fact

If a pull already happened, revoke still matters for the remainder. Read `allowance` on every token you ever approved on each chain you use. Two chains, two lists. Spreadsheets beat memory. This school will not run the revoke for you and will not ask for a seed to ‘batch it.’

lessons.title: Fake tokens and lookalike addresses
lessons.content:
# Fake tokens and lookalike addresses

The alphabet of 0x is small enough for poison: dust from an address that shares your prefix and suffix so a hurried copy from history grabs the attacker. Homoglyphs and similar-prefix contracts sit beside them.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to copy from a bookmark or check first and last four characters of an 0x, and treat famous names on wrong contracts as bait.

## Poisoning

You once sent to a friend. An attacker sends you 0 of a junk token from an address that looks like the friend in the history UI. You copy the from-address of the junk row. You just set a drain destination. Copy from your address book, not from a surprise incoming.

## Lookalike tokens

Same decimals, same logo, wrong 0x. Fake USDT. Fake CST. Identity is academy 0x on chain 56. Cheap gas on BSC makes these cheap to spawn. Dear gas on Ethereum does not prevent them.

## Clipboard malware

Some malware swaps a copied 0x in the clipboard. Check first and last four on the device screen before you sign. Hardware wallets help only if you actually read the destination.

TABLE
Trick | What you copy | Defence
Poison dust | History row of junk | Address book / bookmark
Fake USDT/CST | Logo in wallet | Canonical 0x per chain
Clipboard swap | Pasted destination | First/last 4 on device
Homoglyph UI | Lookalike site | Bookmarked origin
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
HISTORY
  real friend send
  junk dust from lookalike 0x
Copy the junk from-address --> future sends go to attacker.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: staff will not send you a token to ‘test copy-paste.’ Incoming surprise tokens are hide-and-ignore.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Poisoning uses history UIs.
- Logos are not 0x.
- Fake CST is expected.
- Check first and last 4.
- Clipboard malware exists.

Next: proxies, pause, and the renounce sticker.
## First/last four is not paranoia

`0x1234...abcd` versus `0x1234...abce` is enough. Poison addresses are built to pass a tired glance. Hardware screens that truncate the middle are why the glance has to be the ends **and** a bookmark. For CST, do not use ends-only: use the full academy 0x on chain 56 from materials, not from a history row.

## Same 0x, wrong chain

Pasting the academy CST 0x into an Ethereum explorer is not verification. It is a different computer. Fake tokens also copy the 0x **shape** onto chain 56 with different bytes. Chain ID plus full 0x, from materials, or you are sightseeing.

lessons.title: Proxies, pause, and the renounce sticker
lessons.content:
# Proxies, pause, and the renounce sticker

A proxy lets admin point the same 0x at new bytecode. `pause` can freeze sells. `renounceOwnership` on the implementation while proxy admin lives is a sticker on the wrong door.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name proxy admin as a remaining person, and treat pause as an exit freeze until you read who holds it.

## Species

Transparent, UUPS, beacon. All of them mean: the 0x you bookmarked may run different code next month. A timelock on `upgradeTo` is a delay. A delay is not a deletion. EOA admin is a person with worse UX than a company.

## pause

If `pause` blocks `transfer` to the pair, the candle can still print from excluded addresses while you cannot exit. Reads as a ‘market dump’ in a group chat. It is a function.

## The sticker

Renounce on Ownable at the implementation, tweeted with a screenshot, while ERC-1967 admin can `upgradeTo` a new implementation that mints — costume. Read both 0x. Read remaining roles. Write “not immutable” if any path remains. That sentence is literacy, not an insult.

TABLE
Claim | What would make it true | Costume
Immutable | No upgrade, no mint, no pause, no admin | Renounce screenshot of one slot
Paused sells | pause() + pair blocked | ‘network congestion’
Locked LP | locker contract, time, no owner withdraw | Label on an EOA
Timelock | Cannot skip delay | Admin is the timelock owner who can cancel and replace
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
PROXY 0x  --upgradeTo--> new bytecode
ADMIN 0x  still live?
IMPLEMENTATION owner renounced?  <-- sticker often lives here
Read the admin slot anyway.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: you will not be asked to bless a token because it is ‘renounced.’ You will be asked whether any other door remains.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Proxies change bytecode later.
- Timelock is delay, not deletion.
- pause can freeze exits.
- Renounce can be the wrong contract.
- Write remaining doors, dated.

Next: support theatre and the never-list.
## Two 0x memo

Write: proxy 0x, implementation 0x, admin 0x, pause holder, mint role. If any field is “not found, unverified,” write that — do not write “renounced.” A tweeted screenshot of `owner() === 0x0` on the implementation is one field of five.

Upgrade delay 24h is a window to exit if a market exists. It is not a promise they will not upgrade.

## Pause holder as government

Who calls `pause`? An EOA is a person. A multisig is people. A ‘community’ with no 0x is a poster. If pause exists, write the holder in the same memo as mint and upgrade. DAOs course will reuse that sentence for governors.

lessons.title: Support theatre and the never-list
lessons.content:
# Support theatre and the never-list

After a failed transaction or a drain, a helpful stranger arrives. They need a seed to ‘sync the validator’, a 2FA code to ‘unlock the ticket’, remote desktop to ‘install a fix’, or CST to ‘pay the gas queue.’ That is the second product. This school will not sell it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to recite the never-list and the tuition rails without looking, and treat recovery DMs as hostile.

## Never

Seed phrase. Private key. Authenticator / 2FA codes. Remote control (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, and cousins). ‘Validator sync.’ Gas prepay in CST. Sending BNB to a chat 0x to ‘speed a nonce.’ Connecting a wallet to a ‘verify certificate NFT’ page. Paying Intermediate to a Telegram address.

## Recovery is not a function of this computer

Public pages do not unwrite because someone is sorry. Explorers do not have a help desk that can reverse your signature. A company CEX might freeze a row if you still have an IOU there — that is their product, not the chain’s, and not this academy’s.

## What this academy will do

Teach the objects. Take $10 USDT BEP-20 on checkout for Intermediate. Point at CST `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on chain 56 as verify-only. Store your progress as a login. Never custody your key. Next course (DeFi) names the gun `allowance` in full.

TABLE
Ask | From academy? | From a drain
USDT on checkout origin | Yes | Clone origin + different 0x
Seed to sync | Never | Always
CST as gas | Never | Common
Remote desktop | Never | Common
Quiz / lesson | Yes | Fake PDF / command
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
DRAIN --> panic Google / DM
       --> second signature
Paper never-list before you need it.
Staff will not ask. Mentor will not recover.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rule: write the never-list on paper. Future-you in a hurry is the threat. DeFi next will not make this list shorter.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Never seed, key, 2FA, remote.
- Never CST as gas or tuition.
- Recovery DMs are the second drain.
- Checkout stays on academy origin.
- Allowance is the next course’s gun.

Next: DeFi — programs holding inventory.
## Paper, not memory

Write five lines on paper: no seed; no 2FA to chat; no remote; no CST as gas; checkout only on academy origin in USDT BEP-20. Haste is the product many rooms sell. The public computer will still be here tomorrow. A signature will not.

If Mentor ever asks for a key, it is a malfunction or an impersonation. Report. Do not debug it with a live seed.
